More fundamentally, Vistra's equity re-rating has already capitalized significant hyperscaler optimism at current trading levels; the stock does not re-rate further if the PPA pipeline stalls or if AI data centre load growth slows before additional signed offtake agreements are in place.

The most consequential single event within the next twelve months is the PJM 2027-2028 capacity auction. The June or July 2026 clearing result will set the structural earnings rate for the Energy Harbor PJM fleet — Davis-Besse, Perry, Beaver Valley 1 and 2 — through June 2028, covering the two most material years of the Energy Harbor acquisition payback period. A clearing level that confirms the 2025-2026 repricing was structural removes the principal remaining bear case overhang on the acquisition ROI: at that point, the $3.4 billion cash consideration and debt assumption would be well on the way to being validated by the accumulated PJM capacity and energy margin alone, independent of any hyperscaler premium. A clearing level below the prior cycle, by contrast, would reopen the question of whether Vistra overpaid for PJM nuclear exposure at the top of a one-cycle capacity price spike — a narrative that bears would press aggressively into any subsequent earnings disappointment.

chapters.title: Additional hyperscaler PPAs, ERCOT structural growth, and the 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## The pipeline that follows the template

The May 2024 Microsoft Comanche Peak power purchase agreement did not close a chapter — it opened one. For the first time, a US merchant nuclear operator had demonstrated that a hyperscaler would sign a multi-year offtake contract for existing nuclear capacity at scale, accepting the operational and scheduling terms that merchant generators require. Vistra Corp had set the template; the question that would define the 2026-2030 investment thesis was whether the company could convert that template into a portfolio of contracted cash flows large enough to re-rate the stock from a cyclical merchant to something closer to a regulated utility with a growth overlay.

On multiple earnings calls through 2024 and into 2025, James Burke, who assumed the chief executive role on 1 August 2022, indicated that discussions with additional hyperscalers were active across the fleet. The Microsoft agreement covered Comanche Peak capacity in Texas, where geographic proximity to the rapidly expanding North Texas and Central Texas data centre corridor made the deal structurally coherent. The Energy Harbor nuclear assets in Ohio and Pennsylvania — Davis-Besse, Perry, and the two Beaver Valley units — sit inside the PJM footprint, which by 2025 had itself become a contested arena for hyperscaler power procurement as Virginia and Ohio data centre development accelerated. Burke and his chief financial officer, Kristopher Moldovan, positioned the company as having a 6.4 GW nuclear fleet capable of supporting multiple bilateral offtake conversations simultaneously, a positioning that no other US merchant operator could match at comparable scale outside of Constellation Energy.

## ERCOT: structural demand, not a cycle

Texas became the central battleground for AI data centre power procurement for a cluster of reasons that favoured Vistra's existing asset base: permissive land use, competitive power markets, access to ERCOT's rapidly evolving capacity mechanism, and a state political environment broadly supportive of large industrial load. ERCOT's long-range load forecasts were revised upward repeatedly through 2024 and 2025, with new large loads — predominantly data centre campuses of 100 MW or more — connecting or contracting at a pace that strained interconnection queues.

Vistra's ERCOT generation fleet — anchored by Comanche Peak's 2.4 GW of firm zero-carbon baseload, supplemented by a large gas-fired generation portfolio spanning combined-cycle and peaking assets — was positioned to capture the incremental demand through both retail and wholesale channels. TXU Energy, the company's Texas retail brand serving roughly five million residential and business customers, provided a direct channel to commercial and industrial large loads that competitor generators without integrated retail operations lacked. As AI data centre operators increasingly sought bundled power supply arrangements — fixed-price wholesale combined with managed retail service — the integration of TXU Energy's commercial and industrial book with Vistra's generation fleet carried strategic optionality that was not yet fully reflected in external earnings models as of the frozen window.

The ERCOT market's structural evolution also mattered at the regulatory level. Texas legislators and grid operators had been debating dispatchable generation support mechanisms and reliability programmes throughout 2024-2025. Any formalisation of capacity-like payments within ERCOT — even partial — would provide a secondary revenue floor beneath the energy-only market revenues that had made Vistra's ERCOT earnings volatile in prior cycles. The absence of such a mechanism remained a risk, but the direction of the policy debate had shifted toward greater dispatchable generation support as grid reliability concerns from AI load growth intensified.

## PJM and the durability of the capacity uplift

The PJM 2025-2026 capacity auction that cleared in July 2024 at materially elevated prices relative to the preceding cycle represented a step-change in Vistra's PJM revenue run rate. The four Energy Harbor nuclear units — acquired at approximately $3.43 billion including debt assumption and equity consideration — earned capacity revenue that compressed the acquisition payback period relative to the deal's announced economics. The forward question was whether subsequent PJM capacity auctions would sustain those clearing prices, or whether new supply entry — including demand response, imports, and new gas-fired peakers incentivised by the elevated capacity revenue — would erode the clearing level.

The structural argument for durable PJM capacity pricing rested on two pillars: the persistent retirement of coal and older gas assets that had depressed capacity prices in prior auction cycles, and the continued load growth from data centre development in Virginia, Ohio, and adjacent states. Nuclear assets in PJM, including the Energy Harbor fleet, benefited from zero-emission credits in certain PJM states and the federal Section 45U production tax credit, meaning their effective floor economics were substantially better than unaided merchant margins. That combination — state-level support, federal PTC floor, and elevated capacity clearing — gave the Energy Harbor assets a layered revenue structure that made them resilient to individual market moves.

| Revenue stream | Asset type | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| PJM energy market | Nuclear + gas | Ongoing, market-priced |
| PJM capacity revenue | Nuclear (Energy Harbor) | Auction-by-auction, 1-3 year clearing cycles |
| Section 45U PTC floor | All nuclear (6.4 GW fleet) | Through 2032, IRA-statutory |
| Microsoft Comanche Peak PPA | Comanche Peak nuclear | Multi-year, undisclosed term |
| State zero-emission credits (Ohio, Pennsylvania) | Davis-Besse, Perry, Beaver Valley | Subject to state legislative renewal |

## Nuclear license renewal and the 45U horizon

All six of Vistra's nuclear reactors will require either licence extension or operational continuity decisions within the 2026-2030 window and beyond. Comanche Peak Units 1 and 2 hold operating licences extending to 2030 and 2033 respectively. The Energy Harbor fleet — Davis-Besse, Perry, Beaver Valley 1, and Beaver Valley 2 — carries licences that extend into the 2030s and 2040s under existing NRC terms, with further licence renewal applications potentially extending operational lives to 80 years, following industry precedent established by other fleet operators.

The Section 45U production tax credit, enacted under the Inflation Reduction Act, provides nuclear generators a credit that effectively floors revenue on zero-marginal-cost output through 2032. For Vistra's 6.4 GW nuclear fleet — approximately 50 to 52 TWh of annual nuclear generation — the PTC creates a meaningful earnings floor that was not present in the pre-IRA operating environment. The critical policy risk on the long horizon is the 2032 PTC sunset: without extension, the nuclear fleet reverts to fully merchant economics or requires alternative contracted revenue (hyperscaler PPAs, utility offtake, state programmes) to replicate the floor.

## Vistra Vision: the strategic option that hasn't been exercised

The structure of the Energy Harbor acquisition created an entity — Vistra Vision — that is 85% owned by Vistra Corp and 15% owned by Energy Harbor stakeholders who received that minority interest as acquisition consideration. Vistra Vision holds the nuclear fleet (both legacy Comanche Peak and the four acquired reactors) plus the company's renewables and battery storage portfolio. Management indicated that Vistra Vision could serve as a vehicle for additional capital market events: a partial IPO, a minority stake sale to an infrastructure fund, or a further capital raise to fund nuclear-adjacent acquisition.

The IPO optionality was a recurring theme in analyst coverage through 2025. A stand-alone listing of Vistra Vision — holding 6.4 GW of nuclear plus a growing renewables book, with the 45U PTC floor and hyperscaler PPA contracted revenue — could be positioned to a different investor constituency than Vistra Corp's merchant power equity base. Infrastructure funds, pension capital, and ESG-oriented investors seeking zero-carbon baseload with contracted cash flows could represent incremental demand for Vision equity at valuation multiples above Vistra Corp's blended merchant multiple. The timing of any such transaction remained a board-level strategic decision, contingent on market conditions and the pace of additional PPA contracting.

## Capital allocation: returning cash while preserving optionality

Vistra's capital allocation framework through the 2024-2025 period prioritised share repurchases as the primary return mechanism, reflecting management's view that the stock — despite its substantial re-rating from the AI-cycle tailwind — remained undervalued relative to the contracted and semi-contracted earnings embedded in the nuclear fleet. The dividend was maintained at a modest level, with excess free cash flow directed to buybacks. Moldovan and Burke signalled at multiple investor events that the capital allocation preference would continue subject to M&A or Vision-related capital needs.

The Moss Landing battery fire of January 2025 — which damaged the company's 350 MW California lithium-ion storage installation, one of the largest battery storage facilities globally at the time — introduced a discrete capital cost into an otherwise constructive free cash flow picture. Insurance recovery, rebuild decisions, and the broader reputational questions around battery storage fire risk management were unresolved within the frozen window. The incident did not materially alter the nuclear-centred investment thesis, but it added a liability-side complexity to the balance sheet and raised the cost of future large-scale battery storage deployment.

## The central question

Vistra enters the back half of the decade holding a position that would have seemed improbable at its 2016 emergence from Chapter 11: a 6.4 GW nuclear fleet anchored by one of the first hyperscaler PPAs in US merchant power history, a 41 GW total generation portfolio positioned across the two most strategically contested power markets in the country, an integrated retail operation that provides direct access to the commercial and industrial customers driving load growth, and a structural earnings floor from the Section 45U PTC that does not expire until 2032.

The bull case for the 2026-2030 period is straightforward in construction if uncertain in execution: additional hyperscaler PPAs convert the Microsoft Comanche Peak template into a multi-counterparty contracted cash flow portfolio; ERCOT structural load growth from AI data centre development sustains elevated ERCOT energy market revenue; PJM capacity markets clear at levels that reward the Energy Harbor fleet through successive auction cycles; and Vistra Vision crystallises as a discrete capital markets event that surfaces the nuclear fleet's value at a multiple above the blended merchant equity. The Section 45U floor backstops each of those outcomes through 2032.

The risks that can disrupt that sequencing are concentrated but not trivial: failure to execute additional hyperscaler PPAs at acceptable economics; ERCOT regulatory or market design changes that impair energy market revenue; nuclear operational events at any of the six reactors; Moss Landing-derived insurance and rebuild costs that consume capital earmarked for buybacks or Vision; and the long-horizon uncertainty around 45U renewal post-2032. Whether Jim Burke's organisation can sustain the pace of contracting innovation that the Microsoft PPA represented — while managing the operational complexity of a fleet that spans three RTOs, two fuel types of consequence, and six nuclear units — is the execution question that the next four years will answer.

board_of_directors.name: Hilary E. Ackermann
board_of_directors.framing: Ackermann brings public-company governance and finance expertise.

board_of_directors.name: Brian K. Ferraioli
board_of_directors.framing: Ferraioli is a former CFO of major infrastructure construction companies including KBR and Foster Wheeler. The CFO governance experience plus the infrastructure construction perspective is relevant to Vistra's generation fleet operations and the broader infrastructure project execution.

board_of_directors.name: Paul M. Barbas
board_of_directors.framing: Barbas is a former CEO of DPL Inc. (the Dayton Power and Light parent). The utility CEO experience provides peer-CEO governance perspective.

board_of_directors.name: Lisa Crutchfield
board_of_directors.framing: Crutchfield brings utility-industry executive experience including prior senior roles at major US utilities.

board_of_directors.name: Geoffrey D. Strong
board_of_directors.framing: Strong is a former Apollo Global Management partner who provides private-equity operating perspective. The Apollo pedigree connects to the broader US energy private equity network.

board_of_directors.name: John W. Wilder
board_of_directors.framing: Wilder is a former CEO of TXU Corporation — the pre-EFH-bankruptcy predecessor entity. The TXU institutional memory provides historical context for the post-bankruptcy Vistra operating model.

board_of_directors.name: Other independent directors
board_of_directors.role: Additional directors with sector-relevant operational, finance, and governance experience; full slate disclosed in the proxy statement.

leadership.board_composition_observation: Vistra's board pairs Chairman Helm (former Constellation Energy Group executive) with CEO Burke and a slate of directors providing utility-CEO experience (Barbas DPL, Wilder TXU), CFO governance (Ferraioli KBR/Foster Wheeler), private-equity perspective (Strong Apollo), and broader operational and finance backgrounds. The composition reflects the company's post-EFH-bankruptcy origin, the subsequent Dynegy and Energy Harbor consolidation, and the AI capex cycle positioning. The Wilder presence specifically (former TXU CEO from the pre-bankruptcy era) provides multi-decade institutional memory of the Texas competitive electricity market that ERCOT operates within.
